Timothy Chow said:

I have posted a potentially controversial MathOverflow question about whether Lean is the "only game in town."

No it isn't, it's just the most widely known one thanks to Kevin Buzzard hype, Peter Scholze hype, Mochizuki / IUT hype, and LLM hype. Plenty of people using other theorem provers like Rocq and Agda and countless others I can't remember.

Anybody like James Hanson who wants to use a ZFC based proof assistant should go find one right now (there are plenty of those as well) and start developing the mathematics libraries in their proof assistant of choice as soon as possible, lest they fall behind the dependent type theory based proof assistants even more. Anybody trying to get people to use other proof assistants should lead by example, otherwise nobody is going to take them seriously.

The bigger question perhaps is what the mainstreaming of Lean means for the accepted foundational axioms of mathematics, since you're going to need to add some large cardinal axioms to ZFC to make it equivalent in strength to Lean. Is pure ZFC no longer the default then? If so, that's going to overturn 100 years of conventional wisdom regarding the foundational axioms.

Note that most mathematicians don't use ZFC in practice, they use some informal naive set theory with the axiom of choice. Perhaps the rise of Lean just indicates how overrated ZFC is in mathematics, and formal set theory should be downplayed in the mythology and narrative of mathematics.

A historical remark: I pushed for an undergraduate degree in lean precisely because I could not get the other prover communities to take an interest in the project (I was constantly met with comments such as "how do I get a paper out of such work?" or "what is the point? The material is all known to be correct"). The lean community was the only one open to developing a basic coherent mathematics library in the 2010s. Now it's manifestly clear that it was a good idea but I am still not convinced that the idea will be an easy sell in the other prover communities. Even when we were well on the way, the refusals changed, this time to "what's the point in making a coherent undergraduate degree, Lean did it already". Goodness knows I tried to get all the communities building mathematics as I understand it, but the lean community was the only one that listened. If you think you can change that now and get these other communities interested in a system which could support the mathematics behind all modern Fields medals then please go ahead! I am sure that there are plenty more things to be learnt about how to best make such a library. But I tried and I failed, and my obnoxious approach ("obviously the thing to be doing is formalising the things that all the top maths departments are teaching their undergraduates, and not what you are doing"), which in retrospect was extremely clumsy, made me several enemies. I hope you have better luck.

Might be worth reposting that comment over to MathOverflow since there's a discussion between Timothy Chow and WIll Sawin in the comments under the question speculating why you chose Lean over some other proof assistant.

Mark MacDougal said:

The bigger question perhaps is what the mainstreaming of Lean means for the accepted foundational axioms of mathematics, since you're going to need to add some large cardinal axioms to ZFC to make it equivalent in strength to Lean. Is pure ZFC no longer the default then? If so, that's going to overturn 100 years of conventional wisdom regarding the foundational axioms.

People working in certain areas of category theory have been freely assuming at least 2 or 3 inaccessibles for a long time now, so "overturning 100 years of conventional wisdom" is an overly dramatic way of putting it.

I think that to say that ZFC is overrated is a misunderstanding of what its role is supposed to be. Here are some things that ZFC accomplished: (1) It provided an axiomatization that was sufficient for all of mathematics at the time, demonstrating concretely the unity of mathematics and the possibility of rigor in all areas of mathematics. (2) It has remained free from paradoxes, giving us confidence in the soundness of mathematics as a whole, and giving us a clear framework in which to consider questions of consistency. (3) It paved the way for results such as the independence of the continuum hypothesis, and more generally forcing. (4) There's an old joke that the nice thing about standards is that there are so many to choose from. In many situations it is highly convenient to have some standard, whether or not it is "perfect." ZFC has played that role admirably well.

Some of these items, especially (1) and (2), are so taken for granted nowadays that people forget what significant accomplishments they were. Instead, ZFC is expected to play other roles, such as defining what mathematical objects "really are" or capturing the essence of mathematical practice, or defining what axioms are necessary (rather than sufficient) for mathematics. These tasks were not what ZFC was designed for, so it should not be surprising that it is not necessarily optimized for those purposes. But again, to say that ZFC is "overrated" because it isn't optimal for these other purposes is to make the mistake of assuming that that's what ZFC is supposed to be.

Even if you are prepared to take for granted that "of course mathematics is sound" and "of course mathematics is unified," ZFC still plays useful foundational roles today. When people raise questions of consistency strength, calibrating against ZFC and large cardinal axioms still provides the clearest approach.

The rise of Lean has less to do with the alleged superiority of type theory over set theory and more to do with sociological factors, including the fact that most mathematicians don't care about foundations and will judge proof assistants based on their user experience. If Lean gives them a good user experience, then they will happily use it, even if they don't have the faintest idea what the underlying assumptions are.

Timothy Chow said:

(1) It provided an axiomatization that was sufficient for all of mathematics at the time, demonstrating concretely the unity of mathematics and the possibility of rigor in all areas of mathematics.

The thing was that ZFC wasn't sufficient for all of mathematics at the time (1920s, 1930s). You have the constructivists and intuitionists such as Brouwer, Weyl, Kolmogorov, etc around the same time who just flat out rejected excluded middle and assumed axioms that contradicted excluded middle and the axiom of choice, and were able to develop mathematics that we now know is consistent. So ZFC failed if its goal was to demonstrate the unity of mathematics.

The situation has gotten even worse regarding the unity of mathematics since the 1930s, with the proliferation of many more non-classical first-order logics such as affine logic and paraconsistent logic that mathematicians work in to develop set theory and mathematics, and of many other set theories in classical first-order logic that mathematicians do work in that are contradictory with ZFC, such as the Solovay model and the people who assume the axiom of determinacy. And now there are the large cardinal axioms being implicitly used whenever a mathematician regards a Lean proof as valid.

The large cardinal axioms needed to make ZFC equivalent to Lean just forces the issue of the lack of unity in mathematics front and center. One has to adopt a viewpoint like the set theoretic multiverse in order to maintain some semblence of unity in mathematics (which is to say, ZFC should not be considered the foundations of mathematics), and even then I say that Hamkin's multiverse isn't big enough to accommodate all of mathematics, and one really needs to have something like the empty theory rather than ZFC be the basepoint of the set theoretic multiverse.

@Mark MacDougal the point was made about wanting to avoid DTT. I'm aware of HOL-based ITPs, but since "all mathematics is founded on set theory", people really do think that using a ZF-based formalisation system is sensible (cough Harvey Friedman sounding off about formalisation in HoTT vs "real mathematics")

I was under the impression, considering comments made in this MathOverflow discussion and past answers Timothy Chow made on MathOverflow such as this question, that it's not just wanting to avoid DTT, but also that Lean is not equivalent to ZFC and people want a theory equivalent in strength to ZFC.
But the most important point is probably expressed by Timothy Chow above, "the fact that most mathematicians don't care about foundations".
So it may very well just be a small minority of mathematicians that care about foundations.

Timothy Chow said:

(2) It has remained free from paradoxes, giving us confidence in the soundness of mathematics as a whole, and giving us a clear framework in which to consider questions of consistency.

Depends on your definition of paradox. ZFC implies the Banach-Tarski paradox for instance; perhaps you might have meant contradiction instead of paradox.

So at best it's really about:

  1. ZFC provided an axiomatization that was sufficient for most of mathematics at the time, demonstrating concretely the possibility of rigor in most areas of mathematics.
  2. ZFC has remained free from contradictions, giving us confidence in the soundness of most of mathematics, and giving us a clear framework in which to consider questions of consistency.
  3. ZFC paved the way for results such as the independence of the continuum hypothesis, and more generally forcing.

James Hanson's last paragraph says

For example, Mathlib's category theory library is notoriously awful to use because it runs into all this obnoxious bureaucracy involving managing definitional equality, universes, transport, coherence, and typeclass inference. (Consider for example, the mathematically trivial bookkeeping lemma CategoryTheory.shiftFunctorAdd'_assoc, whose theorem statement is so complicated it contains two inline proof scripts.) Having a smooth user experience for category theory would be a fundamental design goal of my ideal proof assistant, because category theory is a fundamental tool in many parts of mathematics. This would be important enough to potentially motivate very low-level changes to the implementation of the system. But I also wouldn't use categorical foundations because (and, again, someone is going to get mad at me for saying this), categorical foundations are actually pretty bad and difficult to use in practice.

I think the answer to this would be to abandon the idea of general proof assistants and start shifting towards domain specific languages for different branches of mathematics, such as a specific language / proof assistant for category theory, while you still get your set theory / type theory based proof assistants for stuff like point-set topology which aren't so well expressed in the category theory proof assistant. This will also be a valid option for "alternatives to Lean".

Mark MacDougal said:

So ZFC failed if its goal was to demonstrate the unity of mathematics.

I think this amounts to quibbling. It's easy to forget nowadays what it was like back in the days of, say, Cauchy, when analysis seemed to be a different subject from arithmetic, with strikingly different methods of reasoning, and arguments about whether calculus was rigorous. It's also easy to forget how much people like Frege and Russell struggled to clarify foundations, and avoid paradox. Even your example of intuitionism is not really a counterexample; as you said, intuitionistic proofs are valid in ZFC, so they still fall under the big tent.

Later developments also don't demonstrate the disunity you claim. Nonclassical logics can be studied, and typically are studied, using classical mathematics. Nor are large cardinal axioms a "threat"; quite the contrary. It's only because of our robust understanding of sets, based on ZFC, that we have such a clear understanding of large cardinal axioms. People can argue about whether they're true, but we all know that those are philosophical rather than mathematical issues, since the mathematical picture is clear: some things require a large cardinal axiom and other things don't.

Again, I think you are taking an insular view of the role of ZFC. It provides unity not in the sense that everyone accepts classical logic or its axioms. It provides unity in the sense that we know that all valid mathematical arguments can be formalized in ZFC, possibly conditional on a clearly identifiable additional axiom. Once again, I maintain that the fact that we take all these things for granted to the point where they seem invisible, is itself a demonstration of how successful ZFC has been.

Mark MacDougal said:

I think the answer to this would be to abandon the idea of general proof assistants and start shifting towards domain specific languages for different branches of mathematics, such as a specific language / proof assistant for category theory, while you still get your set theory / type theory based proof assistants for stuff like point-set topology which aren't so well expressed in the category theory proof assistant. This will also be a valid option for "alternatives to Lean".

I don't have any objection to domain-specific proof assistants, but they would fail to fulfill the purpose that a lot of people are wanting proof assistants to fulfill. People want a way to mechanically validate arbitrary mathematical results. The unity of mathematics means that many theorems can't be pigeonholed into a specific domain. If the proof of a particular theorem requires both point-set topology and category theory, then presumably neither your specialized point-set topology proof assistant nor your specialized category theory proof assistant will be able to cope with it.

Let me try to put the point another way. Everyone believes that any correct mathematical proof can be formalized in Lean, with enough patience. But why does everyone believe this? How can you know in advance that some area of math that hasn't yet been formalized will present no fundamental difficulties? I maintain that the reason is that we know that math is math. And how do we know that? It's because in the 20th century, people figured out that all of math can be formalized set-theoretically. Of course, once you figure out that "math is math", you don't necessarily have to formalize everything in set theory. If you show that, say, type theory and set theory are mutually interpretable, then you can switch over to type theory if you prefer, and still know that "math is math" and everything can be formalized in type theory. But this insight is still ultimately piggy-backing on the original hard work that was done to show that there is at least one common foundation for all of math.

Timothy Chow said:

Let me try to put the point another way. Everyone believes that any correct mathematical proof can be formalized in Lean, with enough patience.

That is just factually untrue. The HoTT people don't believe that proofs done in HoTT can be formalized in Lean, because Lean bakes the UIP axiom into their system, which contradicts the univalence axiom that HoTT people use.

And no, building a model of homotopy type theory inside of Lean does not count, people don't really want to build a model of their preferred foundations inside of Lean to work with their preferred foundations. Otherwise, there would be no objection to building a model of ZFC inside of Lean and then simply proving everything inside of that model of ZFC in Lean.

On second thought, why not just build a model of ZFC inside of Lean and then simply prove everything inside of that model of ZFC in Lean? It's the same idea as Isabelle/ZF, only it's inside Lean instead of Isabelle. Isabelle is fundamentally also based on type theory instead of set theory.
It sounds like we're now in agreement? "Building a model of ZFC inside of Lean" is basically what I was alluding to when I referred to mutual interpretability.
Isn't this docs#ZFSet
Looks like Lean already has a model of ZFC in its library: https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/SetTheory/ZFC/Basic.html
Should be possible to start constructing stuff like real numbers and Banach spaces and proving the Banach-Steinhaus theorem inside of that model of ZFC.

It looks like Mark MacDougal wrote a paragraph about HoTT, crossed it out, and then uncrossed it out. Again, I think this comment about HoTT misses the point. Sure, Lean is proof-irrelevant, so we can't replicate HoTT in Lean naively. Does that mean that Lean users are helpless if they want to verify the correctness of researchers in HoTT? Of course not. In the worst case, they can build an entire HoTT microcosm inside of Lean, and check the correctness of proofs that way. It would be painful, and hardly anyone would want to do this in practice, but that's not the point. The topic of discussion is not the efficiency or practicality of using this or that proof assistant for formalizing this or that particular piece of mathematics. The topic of discussion is the unity of mathematics, and the source of our confidence in that unity. HoTT researchers aren't doing anything so radically different that we can't recognize it as math, and are absolutely incapable of verifying the correctness using our favorite general-purpose proof assistant. Math is math, and HoTT is no exception, so we are highly confident in advance that we can handle it in principle (not saying anything about how painful it might be). And historically, the reason we know that math is math is that we figured out how to reduce everything to set theory. Nor is set theory a purely accidental choice here. It's precisely because sets are so "simple" that they have the protean flexibility to model all other mathematical work easily.

Once again, all this is, or should be, completely obvious to the point that it's hardly worth stating explicitly. However, just because people don't bother to state these obvious facts explicitly doesn't mean that they are any less true.

Timothy Chow said:

Even your example of intuitionism is not really a counterexample; as you said, intuitionistic proofs are valid in ZFC, so they still fall under the big tent.

Depends on whether you accept anti-classical axioms, and even if you don't, a mere validity kinda misses the point. In dependent type theory you can have a distinction between propositions and constructions.

This said, if validity is the only concern, then ZFC is an excellent common ground.
